1. Introduction to Streaming in Node.js
When you work with files, APIs, or network sockets in Node.js, you’ll often face situations where the data is too large to be processed all at once. Think of uploading a video to YouTube, downloading a 5GB file, or transferring logs from one service to another.
Traditionally, you might read the entire file into memory using something like fs.readFile(), process it, and then write the result somewhere. But this approach quickly becomes inefficient and can crash your system if the file size exceeds your available memory.
Node.js provides an elegant, powerful mechanism to solve this: Streams.
A stream is a sequence of data that is being read from or written to continuously over time. Instead of waiting for the entire file or network response to load, Node.js processes chunks of data as soon as they arrive.
This allows you to:
Start processing early without waiting for the full data to load.
Use less memory, since data is handled in chunks.
Handle large files efficiently, even gigabytes in size.
Improve performance in I/O-heavy applications.
Node’s streams are the backbone of many internal modules — such as http, fs, and net. In fact, when you make an HTTP request or read a file, you’re already using streams under the hood.
2. Why Streaming Matters
Let’s take a real-world analogy.
Imagine you’re watching a movie on Netflix.
You don’t wait for the entire movie to download before watching it, right?
You stream it — meaning you start receiving small parts (chunks) of data and start watching immediately.
That’s exactly how streaming works in Node.js.
If you had to download the whole file before using it, your memory would fill up, your app would freeze, and your users would be frustrated. Streaming fixes that.
Key advantages of streaming in Node.js:
Low Memory Usage
Streams handle data in chunks, so Node doesn’t need to load the whole file into RAM.
Faster Data Processing
Processing starts as soon as data starts flowing. You don’t wait for the whole input to arrive.
Efficient for Large Files
Ideal for logs, media files, and database dumps.
Built-In Support
Node.js has native APIs for file, network, and HTTP streaming.
Composable Design
You can combine multiple streams (e.g., read → compress → encrypt → write) using pipes.
This makes streaming perfect for data pipelines, real-time apps, video streaming services, and API gateways that process continuous data flows.
3. How Streams Work Internally
Streams are built on top of EventEmitters, which means they work through events like data, end, error, and finish.
Each stream represents either:
A source of data (e.g., reading from a file)
A destination of data (e.g., writing to a file)
You can imagine it as a pipe system:
[Source: Readable Stream] ---> [Processing: Transform Stream] ---> [Destination: Writable Stream]
Each part handles its own chunk of data as it flows through.
Node.js divides streams into two modes:
Flowing mode – data is read automatically and provided via events.
Paused mode – you manually call stream.read() to get chunks.
When you listen for the data event, Node switches the stream into flowing mode.
Example:
import fs from 'fs';

const stream = fs.createReadStream('example.txt', { encoding: 'utf8' });

stream.on('data', chunk => {
  console.log('Received chunk:', chunk);
});

stream.on('end', () => {
  console.log('Finished reading file.');
});
In this example:
Node starts reading the file in small chunks (by default 64 KB per chunk).
The data event fires for each chunk.
The end event signals when the entire file has been read.
You can also pause and resume a stream:
stream.pause(); // stops emitting data
stream.resume(); // resumes data flow
4. Types of Streams
Node.js defines four types of streams.
Understanding them is crucial for mastering streaming.
1️⃣ Readable Streams
Used for reading data. Example: reading a file, HTTP request body, or database result.
Example:
import fs from 'fs';

const readable = fs.createReadStream('./input.txt');
readable.on('data', chunk => {
  console.log('Chunk received:', chunk);
});
2️⃣ Writable Streams
Used for writing data. Example: writing to a file or sending HTTP responses.
Example:
import fs from 'fs';

const writable = fs.createWriteStream('./output.txt');
writable.write('Hello Stream!');
writable.end();
3️⃣ Duplex Streams
Can read and write simultaneously. Example: network sockets.
import { Duplex } from 'stream';

const duplex = new Duplex({
  read(size) {
    this.push('Hello from duplex\n');
    this.push(null);
  },
  write(chunk, encoding, callback) {
    console.log('Writing:', chunk.toString());
    callback();
  }
});

duplex.pipe(process.stdout);
4️⃣ Transform Streams
A special type of Duplex stream that modifies data as it passes through. Example: compression or encryption.
import { Transform } from 'stream';

const upperCase = new Transform({
  transform(chunk, encoding, callback) {
    this.push(chunk.toString().toUpperCase());
    callback();
  }
});

process.stdin.pipe(upperCase).pipe(process.stdout);
Try typing text in your terminal — you’ll see it converted to uppercase in real-time!
